title: Scikit-fingerprints: Python library for scikit-learn compatible molecular fingerprints and chemoinformatics
author: Jakub Adamczyk, Adam Staniszewski
raw_text: We present scikit-fingerprints, a comprehensive, fully scikit-learn compatible library for molecular machine learning in Python, based on RDKit. Molecular fingerprints and related functionalities are workhorses of chemoinformatics, yet the widely used open-source frameworks are not compatible with the wider Python machine learning ecosystem based on scikit-learn conventions. scikit-fingerprints closes this gap, bringing molecular fingerprints, molecular filters, similarity and distance measures, applicability domain estimation, data splitting strategies, and more under a single, familiar interface. Scikit-learn compatibility means that an entire chemoinformatics workflow, from a raw SMILES string to a deployable model, can be assembled from composable building blocks and can reuse the mature tooling of the surrounding ecosystem. The underlying RDKit code makes it familiar and extensible for custom chemoinformatics use cases. We put a strong focus on unified interfaces, ease of use, computational efficiency, customization, and extensibility. scikit-fingerprints makes molecular machine learning faster to prototype, easier to reproduce, and simpler to deploy.
summary: scikit-fingerprints is a new python library designed to make molecular data processing, specifically using molecular fingerprints, compatible with the popular scikit-learn ecosystem. molecular fingerprints are numerical representations of chemical structures, essential in cheminformatics for tasks like drug discovery and materials science. this matters to you because it demonstrates how specialized domains, like chemistry, are integrating with mainstream machine learning tools. it highlights the importance of interoperability and standardized apis (like scikit-learn's) for making advanced data types accessible for machine learning. you could observe how domain-specific data often needs transformation (like fingerprints) to be used with general ml algorithms, and how libraries bridge these gaps, making cross-domain applications easier.
why: shows how specialized data integrates with mainstream ml, highlighting interoperability.

title: GenAI Added to Google Earth
author: alwa

title: GenRec: Towards LLM-Native Recommendation at Netflix
author: Jimmc414
summary: netflix is exploring a new approach called "genrec," which uses large language models (llms) for recommendation systems. traditionally, recommendations often rely on collaborative filtering or content-based algorithms. genrec suggests that llms can understand user preferences and item characteristics more deeply, potentially generating highly personalized recommendations or even explaining why a particular item is suggested. this is significant for you as it bridges your interest in llms with practical applications like recommendation engines, which are a core part of many data-driven products. you might consider how llms could be fine-tuned or prompted to improve existing recommendation algorithms, focusing on explainability or handling cold-start problems for new users or content.
why: connects llms to real-world recommendation systems, a key ai application.
